newsitem.title: UK: Sheep-cloners PPL says five years to market.
newsitem.headline: Sheep-cloners PPL says five years to market.

text.p: Sheep-cloners PPL Therapeutics say it will be five years before they have a product on the market, but said they were turning their sights to even more controversial technology -- animal-to-human transplants.

PPL Managing Director Ron James said the small biotech company, which stunned the world by cloning an adult sheep named Dolly, would continue to concentrate on creating transgenic animals. These would include sheep, cattle, rabbits and pigs genetically engineered to produce human proteins.
But he warned the technology was still clumsy and unreliable, although he was confident this would improve.
Asked how long before PPL would have a product on the market, James answered: "It's at least five years away."
Announcing its first annual results since the company was listed last year, PPL reported a pre-tax loss of 6.2 million pounds stg ($10 million). Turnover was 2.5 million pounds.
"I think we might see this level of turnover continue," said Richard Cruse, PPL's finance director. "We will also expect to see the 8.25 million stg (in development costs) increase again."

Turnover fell from 4 million stg when Bayer pulled out its support from PPL's lead product, alpha anti-trypsin, a human protein produced in milk from genetically engineered sheep. AAT is about to begin Phase II clinical trials for use in treating cystic fibrosis.

James said PPL hoped to find a partner for AAT by the middle of next year. "Our plan here is to get a partner on board at the end of the phase II trial," he said. "We obviously need to start talking to them before then and we are talking to potential partners now."

James said the company was looking for new ventures. One possibility was producing genetically engineering pigs for use in xenotransplants, from animal to human. The most likely are pig's hearts, as they are a good match for humans in terms of size and function.
Genetic engineering would allow for animals that produced human sugars on the surface of their organs, so human recipients' bodies' would not reject them.
The company has no immediate plans to use its cloning for any marketable product. The cloning technology is still experimental and the company has yet to create a cloned transgenic animal.
James, who was briefing reporters on PPL's first annual results, said the same technology could be used to create pigs that produce human sugars on the surfaces of their organs.
These sugars help the immune system identify foreign agents, so pig organs that produced human sugars would theoretically be recognised as human.
Such pigs have already been created by other companies. But PPL's cloning technology could be used to grow cloned transgenic pigs -- saving a step in the production process.
The British government has declared a moratorium on xenotransplants until all the dangers, such as introducing an unknown virus into people, are studied. But James said this would not affect PPL.

"By the time we get around to trials either the moratorium will have been lifted or we will be able to do them somewhere else," he said. James said he suspected another company, such as Cambridge-based Imutran, owned by Novartis, would be in trials first anyway.

James said he admired the U.S. approach, which would allow for experimental transplants to go ahead, with patients kept in isolation until it was clear whether they were infected with any strange new animal viruses. "That seems to me to be the more logical approach," he said.

Commercial arrangements were under way for marketing AAT, fibrinogen for wound healing, activated protein C with Novo Nordisk, Factor VIIA with Novo Nordisk, Factor IX and two milk products, one a nutritional supplement with Euro Pharma Co and another with Wyeth.
"We're progressing the whole of the pipeline on time and to schedule," James said. ($1=.6215 Stg)
